assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED made a superconducting artificial atom coupled to a microwave resonator a controllable, readable quantum system. It supplies dispersive readout, the strong-coupling regime, and the architecture on which essentially all superconducting quantum processors rest. Original, clear and enormously influential, with consequences across quantum optics, quantum information and sensing.
assessment.attribution: The 2004 proposal (Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin, Schoelkopf) and the 2004 strong-coupling experiment (Wallraff, Schoelkopf and colleagues) are the decisive pair. Proposing Blais for theory, Wallraff and Schoelkopf for experiment is a coherent three-person split. Girvin's theoretical role is substantial and is the main squeeze from the four-name credit; Yale/ETH and Sherbrooke contributions are intertwined. I do not rely on my own Chalmers circuit-QED experience to settle credit.
assessment.maturity: Over two decades of independent replication in many labs and platforms; the interpretation is fully stable. Timing is subtle because the 2025 prize already recognised macroscopic quantum effects in superconducting circuits, but this is a distinct discovery and mature enough to be recognised.
uncertainties: Whether the committee wants a second superconducting-circuit prize so soon after 2025.
Allocation among Blais, Girvin, Wallraff and Schoelkopf is not cleanly separable and I am relying on recalled history rather than verification.
I have professional proximity to this field, which could bias my weighting.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Time-reversal-invariant topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect opened a whole class of matter classified by topology rather than symmetry breaking. The Z2 invariant, protected edge and surface states and the HgTe experiment give a clear prediction-and-confirmation arc with lasting reach into materials, spintronics and topological quantum computing ideas.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele introduced the Z2 classification and the quantum spin Hall proposal; Molenkamp's group observed the effect in HgTe wells after the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction. The listed trio is a natural configuration, though Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Moore, Balents, Fu and the 3D materials experiments (Hasan, Cava) are outside the credited names and the history is contested.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed independently across many materials and probes (ARPES, transport) for over fifteen years; clearly mature and long overdue by usual standards.
uncertainties: Credit boundary with Zhang and collaborators and the 3D topological-insulator discovery is unresolved among the credited names.
Recalled history not independently verified.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum error correction and fault-tolerant computation establish that quantum information can in principle be protected from decoherence, the conceptual basis for scalable quantum computing. Original and fundamental, and increasingly validated by below-threshold and logical-qubit experiments.
assessment.attribution: Shor and Steane gave the first quantum error-correcting codes; Kitaev introduced the toric code and topological fault tolerance. Shor, Steane and Kitaev is a defensible trio, but Calderbank, Gottesman, Knill, Laflamme, Aharonov, Ben-Or and Preskill also made decisive contributions, and the credited set cannot capture all of them.
assessment.maturity: Experimental demonstrations of logical qubits and surface-code scaling have arrived recently and are encouraging but not yet a fully practical fault-tolerant machine. Recognition may be slightly early on the experimental side, but the theory is mature.
uncertainties: Whether this is a physics discovery or primarily computer science and information theory.
Attribution is diffuse and any three-person prize leaves out essential contributors.
Experimental maturity is still developing.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal and its realisation in ion-trap experiments established trapped ions as a leading quantum-computing and simulation platform, with record gate fidelities and long coherence. Clear, concrete and widely adopted.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller proposed the gate scheme in 1995; Blatt demonstrated the gate and scaled ion-trap experiments. Wineland and Monroe are important but not in the credited names, and Wineland already shared a 2012 prize, which complicates the story. The listed trio is coherent.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with decades of independent reproduction. Partial prior recognition in the 2012 prize for quantum control of ions reduces novelty for the committee.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 prize for ion control.
Overlap with B029 and B054 means Cirac and Zoller could be recognised under a different framing.
Recalled history unverified.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene created a tunable platform for correlated insulators and superconductivity from a simple material, spawning the field of moire quantum matter. Highly original and with enormous impact on condensed matter physics.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted the flat bands at the magic angle; Jarillo-Herrero's group observed the correlated insulator and superconductivity in 2018. The three credited names fit a theory plus experiment split well; Cory Dean and others are relevant to hBN-based moire work.
assessment.maturity: Strongly reproduced and rapidly expanding, but the nature of the superconductivity and the correlated states remains unsettled. Experimentally mature enough, theoretically still developing; probably somewhat early.
uncertainties: The pairing mechanism is not understood.
Timing may be premature compared with fields with a longer track record.
Contributions of others in twisted graphene are not captured in the credited set.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution turns a quantum principle (no-cloning, measurement disturbance) into a communications protocol with provable security, and is a flagship application of quantum information. Conceptually clear and original, with real-world deployments including satellite links.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard introduced BB84; Ekert independently proposed an entanglement-based protocol in 1991. All three are natural candidates for a prize; Wiesner's earlier conjugate-coding idea is a historical wrinkle that is not in the credited names.
assessment.maturity: Experimentally demonstrated for decades; practical security with real devices remains a concern, and the physics-versus-engineering weighting is debatable.
uncertainties: Prize-worthiness as physics, as opposed to protocol design and cryptography.
Wiesner's prior idea and attribution priority.
Implementation-security vulnerabilities.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock combined the magic-wavelength lattice idea with narrow optical transitions to reach fractional uncertainty near 1e-18, redefining precision metrology and opening tests of fundamental physics and relativistic geodesy.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength trapping concept; Ye's group drove it to record accuracy. A two-person prize is neat. Hall and Hansch shared the 2005 prize for the comb that makes it possible, and the ion-clock work of Wineland and Rosenband adds nearby credit not in the supplied names.
assessment.maturity: Mature with independent confirmations from several clock labs and international comparisons; the redefinition of the second is still under way, which is a natural timing marker.
uncertainties: Overlap with previous comb and ion-clock recognition.
Whether the committee considers this metrology as a discovery or an engineering achievement.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cavity optomechanics and quantum acoustics demonstrated ground-state cooling, quantum control and entanglement of macroscopic mechanical oscillators, and coupling to superconducting qubits. This is conceptually close to the 2025 theme of macroscopic quantum behaviour and is important for sensing and transduction.
assessment.attribution: Aspelmeyer and Kippenberg are leaders of cavity optomechanics; Cleland demonstrated quantum control of a mechanical resonator coupled to a qubit. Others such as Painter, Teufel, Lehnert, Schwab and O'Connell are not among the credited names and the decisive-first demonstrations are shared.
assessment.maturity: Quantum ground-state and entanglement demonstrations are confirmed in several systems for over a decade; applications are still emerging, so impact is less settled than for the top choices.
uncertainties: Credit is shared among many leading groups and the trio may leave out equally decisive ones.
Impact is currently more demonstration than transformation.
